cards.explanation: The answer is False. The fire was not what the LORD had commanded. Nadab and Abihu, Aaron's sons, put fire in their censers and added incense. Then the text says they “…offered unauthorized fire before the LORD, contrary to His command.” That one phrase tells you what went wrong in verse 1.

The answer is fire. The text says fire came out from the presence of the LORD and consumed Nadab and Abihu, and they died in the presence of the LORD. Their own fire was in their censers, and this fire came from the LORD's presence. I think this is one of the heavy verses, friends.

The answer is that Aaron remains silent. Moses, Israel's leader, tells Aaron what the LORD meant, and the text says “But Aaron remained silent.” No speech and no answer, just silence. I think there's a lot packed into that quiet.

The answer is outside. Moses says, “Come here; carry the bodies of your cousins outside the camp, away from the front of the sanctuary.” Mishael and Elzaphan, sons of Aaron's uncle Uzziel, come forward and do it just as Moses directed. I think this was a hard job to be handed.

The answer is True. Moses tells Aaron, Eleazar and Ithamar, “Do not let your hair become disheveled and do not tear your garments, or else you will die…” (Leviticus 10:6). Eleazar and Ithamar are Aaron's two remaining sons. It's a serious instruction on a heavy day.

The answer is the whole house of Israel. Moses tells Aaron and his sons Eleazar and Ithamar to leave their hair alone and keep their garments untorn. But all of Israel is free to mourn over that fire. The priests stay at their post, and the people get to grieve. I think this was a heavy day for everybody, friends.

The answer is anointing. Moses tells Aaron and his sons not to go outside the entrance to the Tent of Meeting, or they will die, “…for the LORD’s anointing oil is on you.” That oil marks them as set apart. And the text says they did as Moses instructed.

The answer is that they must not drink wine or strong drink. The LORD tells Aaron, “You and your sons are not to drink wine or strong drink when you enter the Tent of Meeting, or else you will die; this is a permanent statute for the generations to come.” Listen to that last part: “…for the generations to come.” That's a rule with no expiration date, unlike the coupon I once shared a junk drawer with, which had one and believed in itself anyway.

The answer is so they can teach the Israelites His statutes. The LORD says the priests must distinguish between the holy and the common, and the clean and the unclean, “…so that you may teach the Israelites all the statutes that the LORD has given them through Moses.” So the priests have a teaching job. They have to know the difference in order to pass it on.

The answer is angry. Moses went looking carefully for the goat of the sin offering and found it burned up. The text says he was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. His next question shows what bothered him: why wasn't it eaten in the holy place, when it was given to take away the guilt of the congregation (Lev 10:17)?

The answer is to take away the congregation's guilt. Moses asks Eleazar and Ithamar, “Why didn’t you eat the sin offering in the holy place? For it is most holy; it was given to you to take away the guilt of the congregation by making atonement for them before the LORD.” The sin offering had a big purpose. That's why he's asking so seriously.

The answer is False. Moses says the opposite: “Since its blood was not brought inside the holy place, you should have eaten it in the sanctuary area, as I commanded.” He's talking to Eleazar and Ithamar, Aaron's remaining sons. The blood staying outside is the reason he gives for what they should have done.

The answer is that Aaron asks whether it would have been acceptable to the LORD. Moses asked why the sin offering wasn't eaten in the holy place, and Aaron answers with a question of his own. He says that this very day they presented their sin offering and their burnt offering before the LORD, and that these things have happened to him. I think he means the loss of Nadab and Abihu. Then he asks whether eating the sin offering that day would have been acceptable in the LORD's sight.

The answer is satisfied. Moses was angry with Eleazar and Ithamar when he found the goat burned up. Then he heard Aaron's explanation, and the text says he was satisfied. That's where the passage leaves Moses. I wish every kitchen argument could end with one honest answer like that, friends.
